study.title: Prenatal Pilates may ease pain; disability and mood effects are less certain
study.evidence_note: Pain, disability, mood and sleep were synthesised from prenatal studies.
study.confidence_note: Full text with tables and GRADE summary was available.
study.impact_line: Prenatal Pilates probably helps pregnancy-related pain, but disability, mood and sleep estimates are less secure and mostly compare against usual care or low-intensity controls.
summary: Pain improved versus control in four RCTs.
Disability improved, but certainty was low and heterogeneity was very high.
Psychological status improved; sleep did not show a clear benefit.
Controls were mostly usual care or weak exercise comparators.

pico.p: Pregnant women with musculoskeletal pain or discomfort
pico.c: Usual antenatal care, no exercise, or other low-intensity controls
pico.o: Pain, disability, psychological status, sleep quality

limits: No direct comparisons with other prenatal exercise.
One non-randomised study contributed to synthesis.
study.bottom_line: This review suggests prenatal Pilates can reduce pregnancy-related musculoskeletal pain and may improve disability and psychological symptoms, but disability, mood and sleep findings remain uncertain because evidence is small, heterogeneous and mostly versus usual care.

results.detail: Four studies, 127 participants. The paper set a pain MID of 0.95 points on VAS; the CI stayed beyond that threshold in favour of Pilates.
Five studies, 286 participants. Different disability scales were standardised; the paper judged the CI wholly beyond the 0.65 SMD threshold in favour of Pilates.
Five RCTs, 289 participants. The CI lay beyond the paper’s 0.65 SMD threshold in favour of Pilates.
Three studies, 204 participants. The CI crossed no effect and the paper said it also crossed the accepted PSQI MID of 3 points.

how_to_apply: Use as a prenatal exercise option when pain is the main complaint.
Expect a supervised or structured programme.
Trials were usually 50 to 60 min, two to three times weekly, for 8 to 12 weeks.
Do not assume it is superior to other prenatal exercise.
Screen for pregnancy exercise contraindications first.
applies_to: Mild to moderate low back or pelvic girdle pain.
Usual-care settings similar to the trials.
not_for: Head-to-head claims versus other prenatal exercise.
Severe obstetric complications or exercise contraindications.

strengths: Search was broad and no language limits used.
Risk of bias and GRADE were assessed.
weaknesses: Publication bias was not formally assessed.
Controls were often usual care or low-dose exercise.
One non-randomised study was included in synthesis.
Self-reported outcomes are vulnerable to expectation effects.
appraisal.funding_conflicts: Supported by Henan Province medical science and technology research project (LHGJ20250671); authors declared none.

domains.reason: Protocol was prospectively registered on PROSPERO.
Search covered five databases, citation screening and no language limits.

domains.support: Results p.8: excluded studies and reasons in supplement.

domains.domain: Risk of bias assessed in included studies
domains.reason: Included studies were assessed with RoB 2.0 by two reviewers.
Random-effects models, multivariate methods and sensitivity analyses were used where needed.
Discussion and GRADE linked conclusions to risk of bias and imprecision.
Formal publication-bias assessment was not performed because no outcome had more than ten studies.

grade.reason: Pain pooled 4 RCTs; only 15/127 participants came from low-quality studies.
I² was 91%, but all 4 trial effects favoured Pilates and CIs overlapped.
Pregnant participants, Pilates, comparators and pain outcomes matched the review question.
Only 127 participants; sample was below the review’s optimal information size of 400.
Only 4 trials contributed pain, so formal assessment was limited and not downgraded by authors.

clinical_significance: Pain: the paper set a clinically meaningful threshold of 0.95 VAS points; the pooled estimate exceeded it.
Disability and psychological status: the paper used a 0.65 SMD threshold and judged both CIs clinically relevant.
Sleep: the CI crossed both no effect and the paper’s 3-point PSQI MID.
Because comparators were mostly usual care or weak controls, the apparent effect may not equal superiority over other exercise.
comparator_fairness: Mostly credible usual-care controls, but not an active, well-matched prenatal exercise comparator.
One control was below the minimal beneficial Pilates dose.
Expectation and contact time were not consistently balanced across studies.
alternative_explanations: Regression to the mean from symptomatic enrolment.
Expectation and placebo effects from exercise participation.
Co-interventions or usual-care differences not fully described.
spin: Authors concluded Pilates is safe and effective, but adverse events were not reviewed.
Benefit was clearer for pain than for disability, mood or sleep, and no head-to-head exercise trials.
fit_with_evidence: Fits the review's own finding that prenatal Pilates may help pain.
The paper itself notes the lack of direct comparisons with other prenatal exercise.
External guideline evidence was unavailable in the supplied source.
external_validity: Moderate fit for pregnant women with low back or pelvic girdle pain in structured programmes.
Less certain for Australian private sports-physio caseloads needing comparison with other exercise options.
Most studies were from non-Australian settings and used tightly defined protocols.
Not a long-term or postpartum evidence base.
would_change_my_mind: A large blinded outcome-assessment trial against an active, dose-matched prenatal exercise comparator showing little or no difference.
Consistent long-term benefit with fewer limitations and better precision.
A head-to-head trial showing Pilates is clearly superior to another credible prenatal exercise programme.

study.patient_explanation: Pilates during pregnancy may help reduce back or pelvic pain, and it might also help mood. The evidence is less clear for sleep, and we do not yet know if it works better than other pregnancy exercise.
open_questions: Is Pilates better than other prenatal exercise?
Are there any harms that were missed?
key_findings: Disability and psychological scores improved, but certainty was low or very low.
Most trials compared Pilates with usual care, not another exercise.
